n: Job replies to Zophar. In this speech he directly challenges the friends’ claim that the wicked always suffer quickly.
Job asks them simply to listen carefully. If they’ll just hear him out, that would be the best comfort they could give.

f.g: Your listening would be your comfort to me.

n: Let him speak — afterward they can go on mocking if they want.

f.g: Allow me, let me.

n: Job’s complaint is not against people but against God’s ways, so of course he is impatient and troubled.

f.g: He is wrestling with God, not merely with his friends.

n: Look at me, he says, and be shocked into silence.

f.w: lay your hand upon your mouth
f.g: A gesture of stunned silence.

n: Even thinking about what he is going to say makes him shudder.

f.w: trembling taketh hold on my flesh
f.g: Job is troubled by the hard truth he is about to state.

n: Job’s big question: why do the wicked live long, grow old, and become powerful? It contradicts Zophar’s whole speech.
Their children grow up and thrive around them — the very blessing Job lost.
Their homes are safe and peaceful; God’s rod of punishment doesn’t seem to touch them.

f.g: A symbol of God’s discipline or punishment.

n: Their herds breed successfully and never miscarry.

f.g: Breeds.
Does not miscarry.

n: Their children skip and play like lambs in a flock.

f.g: A picture of carefree, happy families.

n: They sing to tambourine and lyre and celebrate with flute music.

f.g: A hand drum like a tambourine.
A flute or pipe, not a modern organ.

n: They spend their lives in prosperity and die quickly and peacefully, without long suffering.

f.w: in a moment go down to the grave
f.g: A quick, painless death — something Job, suffering slowly, would envy.

n: Yet these same people tell God to leave them alone; they don’t want to know his ways.
They ask what good it would do to serve or pray to God — the very attitude Satan suspected was behind Job’s faith (1:9).
Job insists their prosperity is not truly in their own control, and he wants no part of their counsel. He questions their success, not God’s goodness.

f.w: the counsel of the wicked is far from me

n: Turning Bildad’s words (18:5-6) into a question: how often does the lamp of the wicked actually go out? Not very often, Job suggests.

f.w: How oft is the candle of the wicked put out!

n: How often are they really blown away like straw and chaff in a storm? Job doubts it happens as regularly as the friends claim.
The friends say God punishes the sinner’s children. Job says the sinner himself should pay so he will know it.

f.w: God layeth up his iniquity for his children

n: Let the wicked see their own ruin and drink God’s wrath personally.

f.w: drink of the wrath of the Almighty

n: After all, once he is dead, why would he care what happens to his family?

f.w: the number of his months is cut off

n: Can anyone teach God, who judges even the highest beings? Job admits God’s wisdom is beyond theirs — his question is about what they observe.
One person dies at full strength, comfortable and secure…

f.g: Completely untroubled.

n: …well fed and healthy to the very bones.

f.g: Probably “his body is well nourished” (the Hebrew is uncertain).
Full of vigor and health.

n: Another dies bitter, never having enjoyed good things.
Both end up the same — in the dust, covered by worms. Death does not seem to sort people out by righteousness.

f.w: lie down alike in the dust

n: Job knows what the friends are thinking and the schemes they are plotting against him.

f.g: Plans, schemes.

n: They hint, “Where is the great man’s house now?” — meaning Job’s ruined estate proves his wickedness.

f.g: A thinly veiled reference to Job’s own fallen household.

n: Job tells them to ask travelers who have seen the world; they know the facts.

f.g: Signs, evidence, reports.

n: Travelers report that the wicked are often spared in the day of disaster. (Some translations read “spared,” others “reserved” for later judgment.)

f.w: reserved to the day of destruction
f.g: The Hebrew likely means the wicked are spared in calamity — or that their punishment is delayed until a future day.

n: Who dares to accuse a powerful wicked man to his face or repay him for what he has done?

f.w: declare his way to his face
f.g: Confront him openly about his conduct.

n: He is carried in honor to the grave, and a watch is kept over his tomb.

f.g: Literally “watch is kept over the tomb” — an honored burial.

n: Even the soil of his grave is gentle to him, and crowds join his funeral procession, just as countless went before.

f.g: The earth of the burial valley.

n: Job concludes: their comfort is empty, because their answers are false. Their neat theology doesn’t match reality.

f.g: Faithlessness or treachery — their answers betray the truth.
